title: DNA Analysis (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand what DNA tests can and cannot tell you, how samples are handled, and how to protect privacy and dignity. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain DNA, genes and the main kinds of tests in plain words.
Read a sample report and say what it does and does not mean.
Weigh benefits and risks of sharing genetic data.
task: Produce a two-page plain-language explainer on DNA testing with a risk list and a consent checklist.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. You will not handle real samples or interpret anyone's results.
standard: Facts are correct and sourced; limits are stated; no diagnosis is offered; privacy risks are named; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Lab assistants, health communicators, teachers, curious adults.
modules: DNA in simple words
Understand
DNA is the instruction code in cells.
Genes are sections of DNA; we inherit them from parents.
Most traits come from many genes and the environment.
A test reads some parts, not everything.
Height depends on many genes and on food and health in childhood.
Draw a simple DNA to trait picture.
Picture has no false claims.
Kinds of tests
Understand
Tests differ in purpose.
Ancestry, health risk, carrier, paternity, forensic.
A test result is a probability, not destiny.
Medical tests belong with a clinician.
A carrier test shows chance of passing on a condition, not that a child will have it.
Compare three test types in a table.
Table states purpose and limit.
From sample to result
Analyse
Many steps can go wrong.
Collect, label, store, extract, read, report.
Chain of custody records who held the sample.
Contamination and labelling errors cause false results.
A mislabelled tube swaps two results; a barcode check prevents it.
Map the steps and risks.
Every step has a quality check.
Reading a result
Analyse
Results need context.
Percent and risk numbers explain chance, not certainty.
Variants of uncertain meaning are common.
Only a genetic counsellor or clinician explains health results.
A report says a 1.5 times higher chance; absolute risk goes from 2 to 3 in 100.
Explain a sample number to a peer.
Peer repeats it correctly.
Marketing and overclaims
Evaluate
Be careful with big promises.
Beware "find your perfect diet by DNA" or "know your talent".
Look for evidence, regulation and independent reviews.
Price does not prove quality.
An ad claims a diet plan from DNA; no study is shown. The learner marks it as unproven.
Review two adverts.
Overclaims named with reasons.
Privacy and family impact
Evaluate
Your DNA reveals things about relatives.
Data may be sold, hacked or used by insurers in some places.
Findings can surprise families, such as unknown relatives.
Consent must be informed and free.
A family agrees before testing that no one will be told surprises without a counsellor.
Write a consent checklist.
Eight clear questions.
Ethics and fairness
Evaluate
Genetic data must not be used to discriminate.
No test should be forced by employers or schools.
Respect culture and faith views.
Data from some groups is underrepresented, so results can be less accurate.
A study notes fewer data from certain populations and urges wider sampling.
Discuss two cases with peers.
Peers reach a reasoned view.
Write the explainer
Create
Combine all parts.
Use short sentences.
Add a glossary and a where-to-get-help box.
Test with a non-expert.
A reader says, "Now I know to ask a counsellor, not a website."
Finish and test.
Reader can state three limits of DNA tests.
quiz: What is DNA?
The instruction code in cells. (Covered in module 1: DNA in simple words. To pass that module: Picture has no false claims.)
Is a result destiny?
No; it is a chance. (Covered in module 2: Kinds of tests. To pass that module: Table states purpose and limit.)
Name two test kinds.
Ancestry and carrier (or health risk, paternity). (Covered in module 3: From sample to result. To pass that module: Every step has a quality check.)
Why chain of custody?
To show who held the sample. (Covered in module 4: Reading a result. To pass that module: Peer repeats it correctly.)
Who explains health results?
A genetic counsellor or clinician. (Covered in module 5: Marketing and overclaims. To pass that module: Overclaims named with reasons.)
Name one marketing red flag.
A big promise with no evidence. (Covered in module 6: Privacy and family impact. To pass that module: Eight clear questions.)
Why does DNA affect relatives?
Relatives share genes. (Covered in module 7: Ethics and fairness. To pass that module: Peers reach a reasoned view.)
Name a data risk.
Sale, hacking or misuse by insurers. (Covered in module 8: Write the explainer. To pass that module: Reader can state three limits of DNA tests.)
Can employers force tests?
They should not. (Covered in module 8: Write the explainer. To pass that module: Reader can state three limits of DNA tests.)
Why is diverse data needed?
Results are less accurate for under-represented groups. (Covered in module 8: Write the explainer. To pass that module: Reader can state three limits of DNA tests.)
rubric: Clear and tested with a reader
Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others

ladder: DNA in simple words

L1: learner can say what DNA is. Focus module: DNA in simple words (Understand, 2 h). DNA is the instruction code in cells. Key points: Genes are sections of DNA; we inherit them from parents. Most traits come from many genes and the environment. A test reads some parts, not everything.

Teach: open with the worked example. Height depends on many genes and on food and health in childhood. Then set the activity: Draw a simple DNA to trait picture. Mark against the standard: Picture has no false claims. Check at this level: What is DNA? Model answer: The instruction code in cells. Use pictures.
Kinds of tests

L2: learner can name the test kinds. Focus module: Kinds of tests (Understand, 2 h). Tests differ in purpose. Key points: Ancestry, health risk, carrier, paternity, forensic. A test result is a probability, not destiny. Medical tests belong with a clinician.

Teach: open with the worked example. A carrier test shows chance of passing on a condition, not that a child will have it. Then set the activity: Compare three test types in a table. Mark against the standard: Table states purpose and limit. Check at this level: Is a result destiny? Model answer: No; it is a chance. Table of tests.
From sample to result

L3: learner can read a simple report with limits. Focus module: From sample to result (Analyse, 2 h). Many steps can go wrong. Key points: Collect, label, store, extract, read, report. Chain of custody records who held the sample. Contamination and labelling errors cause false results.

Teach: open with the worked example. A mislabelled tube swaps two results; a barcode check prevents it. Then set the activity: Map the steps and risks. Mark against the standard: Every step has a quality check. Check at this level: Name two test kinds. Model answer: Ancestry and carrier (or health risk, paternity). Read a sample result.
Reading a result

L4: learner can check a sample chain. Focus module: Reading a result (Analyse, 2 h). Results need context. Key points: Percent and risk numbers explain chance, not certainty. Variants of uncertain meaning are common. Only a genetic counsellor or clinician explains health results.

Teach: open with the worked example. A report says a 1.5 times higher chance; absolute risk goes from 2 to 3 in 100. Then set the activity: Explain a sample number to a peer. Mark against the standard: Peer repeats it correctly. Check at this level: Why chain of custody? Model answer: To show who held the sample. Trace a sample.
Marketing and overclaims

L5: learner can review ads and consent. Focus module: Marketing and overclaims (Evaluate, 2 h). Be careful with big promises. Key points: Beware "find your perfect diet by DNA" or "know your talent". Look for evidence, regulation and independent reviews. Price does not prove quality.

Teach: open with the worked example. An ad claims a diet plan from DNA; no study is shown. The learner marks it as unproven. Then set the activity: Review two adverts. Mark against the standard: Overclaims named with reasons. Check at this level: Who explains health results? Model answer: A genetic counsellor or clinician. Look at adverts.
Ethics and fairness

L6: learner can coordinate consent records. Focus module: Ethics and fairness (Evaluate, 2 h). Genetic data must not be used to discriminate. Key points: No test should be forced by employers or schools. Respect culture and faith views. Data from some groups is underrepresented, so results can be less accurate.

Teach: open with the worked example. A study notes fewer data from certain populations and urges wider sampling. Then set the activity: Discuss two cases with peers. Mark against the standard: Peers reach a reasoned view. Check at this level: Name one marketing red flag. Model answer: A big promise with no evidence. Show a consent form.
Write the explainer

L7: learner can audit an explainer. Focus module: Write the explainer (Create, 2 h). Combine all parts. Key points: Use short sentences. Add a glossary and a where-to-get-help box. Test with a non-expert.

Teach: open with the worked example. A reader says, "Now I know to ask a counsellor, not a website." Then set the activity: Finish and test. Mark against the standard: Reader can state three limits of DNA tests. Check at this level: Why does DNA affect relatives? Model answer: Relatives share genes. Peer audit.
